chapterTitle: The Rights I Refused — All Things to All Men, and a Crown That Never Withers
themeTitle: “The Freest Man in the Room Made Himself Everyone’s Servant”

scripture.text: Am I not free? Am I not an apostle? Haven’t I seen Jesus Christ, our Lord? Aren’t you my work in the Lord?
scripture.understanding: Four questions, each expecting “Yes.” Am I not ἐλεύθερος — free? Am I not an apostle? Have I not ὁράω — seen — Jesus our Lord? (An apostle had to be a witness of the risen Christ; Paul saw Him on the Damascus road, 15:8.) Are you not my ἔργον, my work, in the Lord? Chapter 9 is not a change of subject from chapter 8. Paul has just said he would give up meat forever for his brother. Now he shows that he has already given up far more: rights he unquestionably had.

scripture.text: If to others I am not an apostle, yet at least I am to you; for you are the seal of my apostleship in the Lord.
scripture.understanding: Some outside Corinth questioned Paul's apostleship. But the Corinthians themselves are his σφραγίς — his seal, the wax impression that authenticates a document. A church that exists because of his preaching is the proof that his commission was real. You do not need a certificate when the building is standing in front of you.

scripture.text: My defense to those who examine me is this.
scripture.understanding: Ἀπολογία — a formal defence in court, the root of our word apologetics. And those who ἀνακρίνω — examine, cross-examine — him are the critics in Corinth. Ironically, the defence he is about to give is not a defence of his rights. It is a defence of his decision not to use them.

scripture.text: Have we no right to eat and to drink?
scripture.understanding: Ἐξουσία — the same word as “liberty” in 8:9. Paul is deliberately using the vocabulary of the strong. Have we no right to eat and drink at the church's expense? Of course we do. The strong in Corinth were insisting on their ἐξουσία to eat idol meat. Paul is about to show them a man who had real rights and laid them down.

scripture.text: Have we no right to take along a wife who is a believer, even as the rest of the apostles, and the brothers of the Lord, and Cephas?
scripture.understanding: Ἀδελφὴν γυναῖκα — a sister as a wife, a believing wife. The other apostles, the Lord's brothers (James, Jude and the others named in Mark 6:3), and Cephas all travelled with their wives and were supported by the churches. This verse tells us Peter was married and that his wife shared his ministry — a detail confirmed by Jesus healing Peter's mother-in-law (Mark 1:30).

scripture.text: Or have only Barnabas and I no right to not work?
scripture.understanding: Barnabas, like Paul, supported himself by working. This is a quiet tribute to Barnabas, Paul's first partner (Acts 13), and it tells us that despite their later disagreement (Acts 15:39), Paul still held him in honour. Neither man was obliged to work; both chose to.

scripture.text: What soldier ever serves at his own expense? Who plants a vineyard, and doesn’t eat of its fruit? Or who feeds a flock, and doesn’t drink from the flock’s milk?
scripture.understanding: Three pictures from ordinary life. No soldier στρατεύομαι — serves in a campaign — paying his own ὀψώνια, rations and wages. No farmer plants an ἀμπελών, a vineyard, and refuses to eat the grapes. No shepherd ποιμαίνω — tends — a ποίμνη, a flock, without drinking its milk. Soldier, farmer, shepherd: all are standard New Testament pictures of ministry. And all of them live from their work.

scripture.text: Do I speak these things according to the ways of men? Or doesn’t the law also say the same thing?
scripture.understanding: Paul anticipates the objection: these are merely human examples. So he turns to Scripture. “Doesn’t the law also say the same thing?”

scripture.text: For it is written in the law of Moses, “You shall not muzzle an ox while it treads out the grain.” Is it for the oxen that God cares,
scripture.understanding: He quotes Deuteronomy 25:4. An ox walking in circles on the threshing floor, trampling the grain, was not to be φιμόω — muzzled — so that it could eat as it worked. Then Paul asks: “Is it for the oxen that God cares?” Of course God cares for oxen (Jonah 4:11 ends with God's concern for the cattle of Nineveh). But Paul's point is that the law's deeper purpose is about people. If God provides for the ox, how much more for the worker in His field.

scripture.text: or does he say it assuredly for our sake? Yes, it was written for our sake, because he who plows ought to plow in hope, and he who threshes in hope should partake of his hope.
scripture.understanding: “Yes, it was written for our sake.” The ploughman ἀροτριάω — ploughs — in ἐλπίς, hope, of a harvest. The thresher threshes in hope of sharing the grain. Every kind of labour is sustained by the expectation of sharing its fruit. Paul reads Scripture as written for the church (compare Romans 15:4).

scripture.text: If we sowed to you spiritual things, is it a great thing if we reap your fleshly things?
scripture.understanding: Σπείρω and θερίζω — sowing and reaping. If we sowed πνευματικά, spiritual things — the gospel, the Spirit, eternal life — is it a big thing if we reap σαρκικά, material things — food, shelter, support? The comparison is deliberately lopsided. What Paul gave them is infinitely more valuable than anything they could give him.

scripture.text: If others partake of this right over you, don’t we yet more? Nevertheless we did not use this right, but we bear all things, that we may cause no hindrance to the Good News of Christ.
scripture.understanding: Others — perhaps Apollos or Peter — had received support from Corinth. Paul had a greater claim. “Nevertheless we did not use this right.” Instead we στέγω — the word means to cover with a roof, and so to bear, to endure, to put up with — all things, so as not to put any ἐγκοπή in the way of the gospel. Ἐγκοπή was a cut in a road, a trench dug to block an advancing army. Paul would rather go hungry than dig a ditch across the gospel's path.

scripture.text: Don’t you know that those who serve around sacred things eat from the things of the temple, and those who wait on the altar have their portion with the altar?
scripture.understanding: “Don’t you know?” Those who serve in the temple eat from the ἱερά, the sacred things; those who προσεδρεύω — attend constantly — at the θυσιαστήριον, the altar, συμμερίζομαι, share in its offerings. This was true in Israel's temple, where priests and Levites lived from the sacrifices (Numbers 18), and it was common knowledge in pagan Corinth too.

scripture.text: Even so the Lord ordained that those who proclaim the Good News should live from the Good News.
scripture.understanding: The climax of the argument: “the Lord ordained.” Διατάσσω — gave orders, commanded. Paul is citing Jesus' own instruction when He sent out His disciples: “the laborer is worthy of his wages” (Luke 10:7). Those who καταγγέλλω — proclaim — the gospel should live from the gospel. It is not merely permitted. It is the Lord's arrangement.

scripture.text: But I have used none of these things, and I don’t write these things that it may be done so in my case; for I would rather die, than that anyone should make my boasting void.
scripture.understanding: Having proved his right beyond doubt, Paul says he has used none of it — and he is not writing to ask for it now. Then a broken, passionate sentence: he would rather die than let anyone κενόω — empty, make void — his καύχημα, his ground for boasting. What is the boast? Not that he preaches; verse 16 says that is no ground for boasting at all. It is that he preaches free.

scripture.text: For if I preach the Good News, I have nothing to boast about; for necessity is laid on me; but woe is to me, if I don’t preach the Good News.
scripture.understanding: Preaching itself is no ground for boasting, because ἀνάγκη — necessity, compulsion — is laid on him. Paul did not choose this vocation; it chose him on the Damascus road. “Woe is to me, if I don’t preach the Good News.” Οὐαί is the cry of the prophets — Isaiah's “Woe is me!” in the presence of God's holiness (Isaiah 6:5). Paul has been seized by a commission he cannot put down.

scripture.text: For if I do this of my own will, I have a reward. But if not of my own will, I have a stewardship entrusted to me.
scripture.understanding: A difficult verse. If he preached ἑκών — voluntarily, of his own initiative — he would have a μισθός, a wage. But he does not: he is under orders. He has been entrusted with an οἰκονομία — a stewardship, the same family as the “stewards” of 4:1–2. A slave-steward does not get paid for doing his duty. So where is Paul's reward?

scripture.text: What then is my reward? That, when I preach the Good News, I may present the Good News of Christ without charge, so as not to abuse my authority in the Good News.
scripture.understanding: Here is the answer, and it is beautiful. Paul's “reward” is the privilege of offering the gospel ἀδάπανος — without cost to anyone. His pay is to work for no pay. That is the one thing in his ministry that is truly his own gift to God, beyond the call of duty. And it keeps him from καταχράομαι — over-using, abusing — his ἐξουσία, his right in the gospel.

scripture.text: For though I was free from all, I brought myself under bondage to all, that I might gain the more.
scripture.understanding: The paradox of Christian freedom in one sentence. Ἐλεύθερος ἐκ πάντων — free from all — yet πᾶσιν ἐμαυτὸν ἐδούλωσα — I enslaved myself to all. The freest man in the room made himself everyone's slave. Why? “That I might κερδαίνω — gain, win — the more.” Freedom is not the right to please yourself. It is the power to serve without being forced.

scripture.text: To the Jews I became as a Jew, that I might gain Jews; to those who are under the law, as under the law, that I might gain those who are under the law;
scripture.understanding: To Jews he became as a Jew — keeping Jewish customs, circumcising Timothy (Acts 16:3), taking a Nazirite-type vow in Jerusalem (Acts 21:23–26). To those under the law, as under the law — “not being myself under the law,” as many early manuscripts add here. Paul's identity was not shaped by the law. But he would adopt its customs to remove obstacles for those who were.

scripture.text: to those who are without law, as without law (not being without law toward God, but under law toward Christ), that I might win those who are without law.
scripture.understanding: To those without the law — Gentiles — as one without the law. Then a crucial parenthesis that guards against misunderstanding: “not being without law toward God, but ἔννομος Χριστοῦ” — under the law of Christ, literally “in-lawed to Christ.” Paul is never lawless. He is bound to Christ and His command of love. Flexibility in culture; no flexibility in obedience.

scripture.text: To the weak I became as weak, that I might gain the weak. I have become all things to all men, that I may by all means save some.
scripture.understanding: The climax of the list, and it connects straight back to chapter 8: “To the weak I became as weak.” Paul did for the weak brother exactly what he asked the strong to do — he limited his own freedom. Then the famous summary: “I have become all things to all men, that I may by all means save some.” Not all men — some. Paul never imagined everyone would respond. But for the sake of some, he would adapt everything except the gospel itself.

scripture.text: Now I do this for the sake of the Good News, that I may be a joint partaker of it.
scripture.understanding: The motive behind all of it: “for the sake of the Good News, that I may be a συγκοινωνός of it” — a co-sharer, a fellow participant. Paul wants to share in the blessings of the gospel alongside those he reaches. He is not standing outside the gospel distributing it. He is inside it, running with everyone else.

scripture.text: Don’t you know that those who run in a race all run, but one receives the prize? Run like that, that you may win.
scripture.understanding: Now an image every Corinthian knew. The Isthmian Games, second only to the Olympics, were held every two years a few miles from the city. Paul may even have been in Corinth during the games of AD 51. In the στάδιον — the stadium, the race course, about 600 feet long — all run, but only one receives the βραβεῖον, the prize. “Run like that” — not lazily, not as a spectator, but to καταλαμβάνω, to seize the prize.

scripture.text: Every man who strives in the games exercises self-control in all things. Now they do it to receive a corruptible crown, but we an incorruptible.
scripture.understanding: Every athlete who ἀγωνίζομαι — competes, from which comes our word agony — ἐγκρατεύομαι, exercises self-control in everything: diet, sleep, training, pleasure. Athletes at the major games swore that they had trained for ten months. And for what? A φθαρτός στέφανος — a perishable wreath. At the Isthmian Games the victor's crown was a wreath of pine, or in some periods of withered celery. It would be brown within a week. “But we an ἄφθαρτος” — an incorruptible one.

scripture.text: I therefore run like that, not aimlessly. I fight like that, not beating the air,
scripture.understanding: Two athletic pictures. A runner who does not run ἀδήλως — aimlessly, without a clear finish line in view. A boxer, πυκτεύω, who does not throw punches at the ἀήρ, the air — shadowboxing, swinging wildly without landing a blow. Paul's life is not a show workout. Every stride is aimed; every blow lands.

scripture.text: but I beat my body and bring it into submission, lest by any means, after I have preached to others, I myself should be rejected.
scripture.understanding: Ὑπωπιάζω — to strike under the eye, to give a black eye; a boxer's word. Paul punches his own body and δουλαγωγέω — leads it as a slave, brings it into submission. He is not despising the body (he has just said it is the Lord's temple, 6:19). He is refusing to let it rule him. And the reason is sobering: “lest… after I have κηρύσσω — preached, heralded — to others, I myself should be ἀδόκιμος” — disqualified, failing the test. The herald who announced the rules of the games could himself be disqualified if he broke them.

visualMeditations.title: The Ox on the Threshing Floor
visualMeditations.image: Picture a threshing floor outside a village in Israel: a circle of hard-packed earth on a hilltop where the wind blows. Sheaves of wheat are spread across it, and an ox walks round and round over them, its hooves breaking the heads of grain loose from the stalks. All day it walks, trampling the harvest. And every so often it lowers its head and takes a mouthful. No one stops it. The law of Moses said, “You shall not muzzle an ox while it treads out the grain.” The animal that does the work shares in what it produces.
visualMeditations.meaning: Paul uses this small law to make a large point: those who labour in the gospel have a right to be supported by those they serve. Jesus said it directly — “the laborer is worthy of his wages” (Luke 10:7) — and Paul calls it something “the Lord ordained” (v. 14). Generous support of those who teach the Word is not charity; it is obedience. But notice the deeper turn in the chapter. Paul proves the right beyond doubt, and then refuses to use it. He would rather go hungry than let anyone say the gospel came with a price tag. Both lessons stand. If you are taught, support those who teach you (Galatians 6:6). If you teach, hold your rights loosely for the sake of the gospel.

visualMeditations.title: The Trench Across the Road
visualMeditations.image: In ancient warfare, when a defending army wanted to slow an advancing enemy, it would dig a deep trench across the road — an ἐγκοπή, a cutting-in. The marching column would grind to a halt at the edge, unable to move forward until the ditch was filled. Paul uses that word in verse 12. He would rather “bear all things” — hunger, weariness, insult, poverty — than dig a trench across the path of the gospel. Picture him at night in his rented room above the tentmaker's shop, hands blistered from the needle and awl, refusing the money that would have made life easier, because he knew someone in Corinth would use it to call him a fraud.
visualMeditations.meaning: Corinth was full of travelling teachers who charged fees and lived well off their audiences. Paul refused to look like one of them. He was willing to give up his legitimate rights — food, a wife's companionship on his travels, financial support — so that nothing about him would become an obstacle to someone hearing the gospel. That is the question this verse asks of you: what in your life might be digging a trench across someone else's road to Christ? Your rights, your comforts, your reputation, your preferences, even good things you are entitled to — are any of them hindering the gospel? Love asks not, “What am I owed?” but, “What is in the way?”

visualMeditations.title: The Withered Wreath
visualMeditations.image: It is the spring of the Isthmian Games, a few miles from Corinth. The crowds pack the stadium. The runners have trained for months — strict diets, early mornings, no wine, no late nights, every muscle disciplined. The starting signal sounds and they explode down the track. One man crosses the line first, his chest heaving, and the crowd roars as a herald places on his head the prize: a wreath of pine, or in some years of withered celery. He wears it proudly. In a week it will be brown. In a month, dust. And down in the crowd, perhaps, a tentmaker is watching, thinking: they do all this for a crown that dies.
visualMeditations.meaning: Paul's point is not that Christians should be athletes but that they should have at least as much purpose and discipline as athletes. Every competitor “exercises self-control in all things” — for a crown that wilts. Believers run for a crown that never fades. And so Paul refuses to run aimlessly or to box the air. He punches his own body and makes it serve him rather than rule him, “lest by any means, after I have preached to others, I myself should be rejected.” The herald who announced the rules could himself be disqualified. If the apostle Paul took that seriously, so should you. Discipline is not legalism. It is love for the prize.

structure.label: Paul's Credentials (v. 1-3)
structure.body: Paul is free, an apostle, a witness of the risen Lord, and the Corinthians are the seal of his apostleship — this is his defence to his critics.

structure.label: The Right to Support (v. 4-14)
structure.body: Paul proves his right to be supported from human example (soldier, farmer, shepherd), from the law (the ox), from fairness (sowing spiritual things, reaping material things), from the temple, and from the command of the Lord Himself.

structure.label: The Right Refused (v. 15-18)
structure.body: Paul has used none of these rights; preaching itself is a necessity laid on him, so his reward is to preach the gospel free of charge.

structure.label: All Things to All Men (v. 19-23)
structure.body: Though free from all, Paul made himself a slave to all — to Jews, to those under the law, to those without the law, to the weak — so that by all means he might save some, for the sake of the gospel.

structure.label: Run to Win (v. 24-27)
structure.body: Like athletes in the Isthmian Games, believers must run with purpose and self-control for an imperishable crown; Paul disciplines his body so that he will not be disqualified after preaching to others.

sections.heading: Proving a Right in Order to Lay It Down
paragraphs: Chapter 9 can look like a digression — Paul suddenly defending his apostleship in the middle of a discussion about idol meat. But it is the heart of the argument. In chapter 8 the strong in Corinth were insisting on their ἐξουσία, their right, to eat idol meat. Paul answered that love might require them to give up that right for the sake of a weaker brother. Now he shows them that he is not asking them to do anything he has not already done himself, on a much larger scale. He uses exactly their vocabulary: ἐξουσία, right, occurs six times in this chapter (vv. 4, 5, 6, 12 twice, 18). And he spends fourteen verses proving that his right was real before he tells them he did not use it.

The argument for support is one of the most thorough in his letters. He appeals to ordinary life — no soldier serves at his own expense, no farmer plants a vineyard without eating the grapes, no shepherd tends a flock without drinking the milk (v. 7). He appeals to the law of Moses — “You shall not muzzle an ox while it treads out the grain” (v. 9, quoting Deuteronomy 25:4) — and insists that it was written for the sake of people. He appeals to justice — if we sowed spiritual things, is it too much to reap material things (v. 11)? He appeals to the temple, where priests lived from the offerings (v. 13). And finally he appeals to the highest authority of all: “Even so the Lord ordained that those who proclaim the Good News should live from the Good News” (v. 14). Paul is almost certainly referring to Jesus' instructions to the seventy-two: “the laborer is worthy of his wages” (Luke 10:7). He quotes both texts together in 1 Timothy 5:18.

Then comes the turn: “But I have used none of these things” (v. 15). Paul's refusal of support was not because he thought it wrong. It was a strategic decision for the gospel's sake. In Corinth, travelling philosophers and teachers were often paid by wealthy patrons, which put the teacher under obligation and made him something like a household dependant. Others charged fees, and the public suspected them of teaching for profit. Paul wanted nothing to suggest that the gospel could be bought, or that he could be owned. He worked with his hands as a tentmaker (Acts 18:3) and accepted gifts from other churches when he was in need (2 Corinthians 11:8–9; Philippians 4:15–16), but he refused to be supported by the Corinthians themselves. Later, his rivals would twist even this against him. But his principle stood: “we bear all things, that we may cause no hindrance to the Good News of Christ” (v. 12).

sections.heading: Free From All, Slave to All: The Shape of Gospel Flexibility
paragraphs: Verses 19 to 23 are among the most quoted in Paul's letters, and among the most misunderstood. “For though I was free from all, I brought myself under bondage to all, that I might gain the more.” This is the paradox of Christian freedom. Paul is the freest man in the room — free from the law as a means of righteousness, free from human masters, free from the opinions of critics. And he uses his freedom to make himself everyone's slave. Freedom, for Paul, is not the right to please yourself. It is the power to serve others without being forced to.

Then he gives examples. To Jews he became as a Jew — circumcising Timothy (Acts 16:3), observing Jewish customs, joining in purification rites at the temple (Acts 21:23–26). To Gentiles, those “without law,” he became as one without the law — eating with them, speaking in their categories, quoting their poets (Acts 17:28). To the weak he became weak — limiting his own freedom so as not to trouble their consciences, exactly as he urged the strong to do in chapter 8. And he sums it up: “I have become all things to all men, that I may by all means save some” (v. 22).

But there are two guardrails here that must not be missed. The first is in verse 21: Paul is never “without law toward God, but under law toward Christ.” He is ἔννομος Χριστοῦ — literally “in-lawed to Christ.” His flexibility is in matters of culture, custom and personal freedom, never in matters of obedience or truth. He would eat with Gentiles, but he would not join their idolatry (chapter 10 makes this explicit). He would keep Jewish customs, but he would never say that keeping them was necessary for salvation (Galatians 2 shows him fighting fiercely on that point). The second guardrail is the goal: “that I may by all means save some.” Paul adapts himself, not the gospel. He changes everything about himself that can be changed, so that nothing but the cross itself remains as an offence. A Christianity that adapts the message to make it comfortable has misunderstood this verse completely. Paul's message never changed. His preferences did.

sections.heading: The Herald Who Could Be Disqualified
paragraphs: The chapter ends with an image the Corinthians knew intimately. The Isthmian Games were held every two years at the sanctuary of Poseidon on the isthmus, a few miles from Corinth. They were second in prestige only to the Olympic Games, and athletes came from all over the Greek world. If Paul was in Corinth from about AD 50 to 52, he may well have been there during the games of 51, perhaps even selling tents to the crowds. So when he writes, “Don’t you know that those who run in a race all run, but one receives the prize?” (v. 24), every reader could picture the stadium. And when he says, “Every man who strives in the games exercises self-control in all things” (v. 25), they knew the rigorous training athletes endured — and the prize they won: a wreath of pine at the Isthmian Games, or in some periods withered celery, that would be brown within days.

Paul's point is the contrast between the crowns. The athletes discipline themselves for “a corruptible crown, but we an incorruptible.” If people will give up comfort and pleasure for months for a wreath that dies, how much more should believers be willing to discipline themselves for a crown that lasts forever? And that discipline is directly connected to what Paul has been saying about rights. The strong in Corinth wanted to exercise every freedom they had. Paul says the Christian life is more like an athlete's training than a banquet: you voluntarily give up good things for the sake of the prize. Self-control is not the enemy of freedom. It is freedom used well.

And then verse 27, one of the most sobering verses Paul ever wrote: “I beat my body and bring it into submission, lest by any means, after I have preached to others, I myself should be rejected.” The verb ὑπωπιάζω is a boxer's word — to strike under the eye, to give a black eye. Paul is not despising his body; he has just called it the temple of the Spirit. He is refusing to let its appetites run his life. And he names his fear: that after acting as a κῆρυξ — a herald, the official who announced the contestants and the rules at the games — he himself might be ἀδόκιμος, disqualified, failing the test. Interpreters differ on whether Paul means loss of his salvation or loss of his reward and usefulness. The word is used elsewhere of people whose faith proves counterfeit (2 Corinthians 13:5; Titus 1:16), and chapter 10 will immediately warn about Israelites who were baptised and fed by God and still fell in the wilderness. At the very least, Paul refused to assume that preaching to others guaranteed his own faithfulness. Neither should you.

ntConnection.heading: New Testament Connection
paragraphs: The principle of supporting gospel workers, which Paul says “the Lord ordained” (v. 14), comes from Jesus' instructions when He sent out the seventy-two: “Remain in that same house, eating and drinking the things they give, for the laborer is worthy of his wages” (Luke 10:7). Paul later quotes both this saying and the ox law together when instructing Timothy about honouring elders: “Let the elders who rule well be counted worthy of double honor, especially those who labor in the word and in teaching. For the Scripture says, ‘You shall not muzzle the ox when it treads out the grain.’ And, ‘The laborer is worthy of his wages’” (1 Timothy 5:17–18). And he tells the Galatians: “But let him who is taught in the word share all good things with him who teaches” (Galatians 6:6). Yet in his own practice, both in Thessalonica and Ephesus, he chose to work: “not because we don’t have the right, but to make ourselves an example to you, that you should imitate us” (2 Thessalonians 3:9). He reminded the Ephesian elders of the words of Jesus, “It is more blessed to give than to receive” (Acts 20:35).

The athletic imagery of verses 24 to 27 runs through Paul's letters to the very end of his life. To the Philippians he writes: “Forgetting the things which are behind, and stretching forward to the things which are before, I press on toward the goal for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 3:13–14). And in his final letter, waiting for execution in Rome, he looks back on the race: “I have fought the good fight. I have finished the course. I have kept the faith” (2 Timothy 4:7). The man who feared being disqualified in 1 Corinthians 9 finished. And the writer of Hebrews gives the whole church the same picture: “let us run with perseverance the race that is set before us, looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith” (Hebrews 12:1–2).

And the imperishable crown of verse 25 is promised by several New Testament writers under different names. James: “Blessed is the man who endures temptation, for when he has been approved, he will receive the crown of life, which the Lord promised to those who love him” (James 1:12). Peter, to elders who shepherd God's flock willingly and not for gain: “When the chief Shepherd is revealed, you will receive the crown of glory that doesn’t fade away” (1 Peter 5:4). And the risen Christ to the suffering church in Smyrna: “Be faithful to death, and I will give you the crown of life” (Revelation 2:10). The wreaths of the Isthmian Games withered in a week. The crown Christ gives does not fade.

lexicon.insight: Strong's: “privilege, i.e. (subjectively) force, capacity, competency, freedom, or (objectively) mastery.” It is the key word linking chapters 8 and 9. In 8:9 the Corinthians' ἐξουσία — their liberty to eat idol meat — threatened to become a stumbling block. In chapter 9 Paul uses the same word six times for his own rights as an apostle: to eat and drink at the church's expense, to take a wife on his travels, to stop working, to be supported. He proves them all. Then he refuses them all. The lesson is that a right is not a command. Having the authority to do something does not mean you must do it. Mature freedom includes the freedom not to use your freedom.

Strong's: “a hindrance.” The word comes from a verb meaning to cut into, and it was used of a trench or obstruction cut across a road to stop an advancing army. This is its only appearance in the New Testament. Paul says he would rather bear all things — hunger, poverty, humiliation, criticism — than put such an obstacle in the way of the gospel. That is a radical standard for ministry. It means asking not merely whether something is permissible, but whether it could slow down someone's journey to Christ. A preacher's lifestyle, a church's spending, a Christian's habits can all become trenches across the road.

Strong's: “to gain (literally or figuratively).” It is a commercial word, used of making a profit in trade — as in Jesus' parable of the talents, where servants “gained” more (Matthew 25:16–17). Paul uses it five times in four verses for winning people to Christ. And Jesus uses it of restoring a brother: “you have gained back your brother” (Matthew 18:15). It reveals what Paul counted as profit. Not money, not comfort, not his rights — people. He gave up everything else in order to gain them. Ask yourself what you are trying to gain with your life. Paul's answer was souls.

Strong's: “to exercise self-restraint (in diet and chastity).” The word comes from κράτος, strength or power, and means to have power over oneself. It was the standard term for an athlete's rigorous training regime: controlled diet, abstinence from wine and sexual activity, early sleep, disciplined exercise. Paul uses the same verb in 7:9 of sexual self-control. The related noun ἐγκράτεια appears in the fruit of the Spirit in Galatians 5:23. Self-control is not grim self-hatred. It is power over yourself for the sake of something you love more than the immediate pleasure. The athlete wants the crown more than the wine. The believer wants Christ more than anything.

Strong's: “unapproved, i.e. rejected; by implication, worthless (literally or morally).” It is the negative of δόκιμος, approved — the word for metal that passes the assayer's test. An ἀδόκιμος coin is counterfeit; an ἀδόκιμος athlete is disqualified. Paul uses it of minds given up to sin (Romans 1:28), of people whose faith is not genuine (2 Corinthians 13:5–7), and of those who are “unfit for any good work” (Titus 1:16). Here he applies it to himself as a possibility to be guarded against. Not because he doubted God's faithfulness, but because he refused to presume on his own. The herald who announces the rules is not exempt from them.

holySpiritRevelation.intro: The Spirit is dealing with three things in this chapter: the rights you are holding onto that may be hindering the gospel, the cultural comforts you are unwilling to leave for the sake of others, and the lack of discipline that could disqualify you.

items.title: What Are You Owed?
items.body: You have rights. Some are legal, some are moral, some are just the reasonable expectations of a person who works hard and serves faithfully. And you may have been insisting on them — in your church, your family, your workplace. Paul had more right than anyone to be paid, honoured and comfortable, and he said: I have used none of these things. Not because the rights were wrong, but because he cared more about the gospel than about what he was owed. The Spirit is asking: what right are you clutching that might be digging a trench across someone else's road to Christ? Could you let it go? Freedom is not getting what you deserve. It is being free enough not to need it.

items.title: Who Have You Refused to Become Like?
items.body: Paul became as a Jew to Jews, as one without law to Gentiles, as weak to the weak. He crossed every cultural line he could cross without compromising Christ. And you? There are people you find hard to be around — a different generation, a different class, a different culture, a different style of faith. You have expected them to come to you, on your terms, in your comfortable world. The Spirit is asking: what would it look like for you to go to them? To learn their language, eat their food, enter their world, lay aside your preferences — all without changing the gospel — so that you might by all means save some?

items.title: Shadowboxing
items.body: You may be busy. Active in church, serving, even preaching to others. But Paul warns about two kinds of wasted effort: running aimlessly and boxing the air. Is your spiritual life aimed at a clear goal, or are you just keeping busy? Is it disciplined, or is it driven by moods? And is there an appetite in your body — food, sleep, sex, screens, comfort — that has been running you instead of serving you? The Spirit is not condemning you. He is calling you into training. Athletes give up good things for a crown that withers. What are you willing to give up for a crown that never fades?

audit.title: The Rights Check
audit.body: List three rights you have insisted on recently — at home, at church, at work. Beside each, ask: if I gave this up, could it help someone see Christ more clearly? Is my insistence on it hindering the gospel in any way? Circle one you could lay down.

audit.title: The Bridge Check
audit.body: Name one person or group you have made little effort to understand because they are culturally different from you. What would it cost you to become “as” them — to enter their world without compromising Christ? What is stopping you?

audit.title: The Training Check
audit.body: Write down your spiritual disciplines over the past month: prayer, Scripture, fasting, giving, service, rest. Then write down one bodily appetite that has been ruling you. Ask honestly: am I running with purpose, or boxing the air?

practices.title: Supporting Those Who Sow
practices.body: Verse 14 says the Lord ordained that those who proclaim the gospel should live from it. This week, do something concrete to support someone who teaches you the Word — your pastor, a missionary, a Bible teacher, a small group leader. Give financially if you can. Write them a specific note of thanks for what you have reaped from their sowing. Pray for them by name. Do not wait for them to ask; Paul's whole point is that the best teachers often will not.

practices.title: A Training Plan for an Imperishable Crown
practices.body: Athletes train for months with a plan. Write a simple thirty-day spiritual training plan. Choose one discipline to strengthen (for example: twenty minutes in the Word every morning before your phone). Choose one appetite to bring under control (for example: no screens after 10 p.m., or one day a week of fasting). Write verse 25 at the top: “they do it to receive a corruptible crown, but we an incorruptible.” Tell one trusted friend about your plan and ask them to check on you weekly. Run with purpose.

prayerReflection: “Lord Jesus, You were free from all, and You made Yourself the servant of all. You had every right in heaven and on earth, and You laid them down for me. Teach me to do the same. Father, I confess that I have clung to my rights. I have insisted on what I am owed, and I have not asked whether my insistence was hindering the gospel. Show me the trenches I have dug across other people's roads to You, and give me grace to fill them in. Let me bear all things rather than put an obstacle in the way of the Good News. Make me all things to all people. Give me the humility to enter the world of people who are different from me, to learn their language, to set aside my preferences — without ever changing the message — so that by all means I might save some. And Lord, keep me under the law of Christ, flexible in culture and immovable in obedience. Holy Spirit, put me in training. I do not want to run aimlessly or box the air. Give me self-control in all things. Where my body has been ruling me, help me bring it into submission, not out of hatred for it, but out of love for the prize. Guard me, so that after preaching to others, I myself am not disqualified. And fix my eyes on the crown that will never fade. In Jesus' name, Amen.”

storyConnections.title: Nehemiah Refuses the Governor's Allowance
storyConnections.summary: Nehemiah was appointed governor of Judah, and the governor was entitled to a food allowance paid for by taxing the people. Earlier governors had used that right and more, laying heavy burdens on the people and letting their servants lord it over them. For twelve years Nehemiah refused the allowance. He fed a hundred and fifty officials at his own table out of his own resources, and he worked on the wall himself. His reason was simple: the burden on the people was already heavy, and he feared God. Nehemiah had a legitimate right, and he refused it so that the work of God would not be hindered by resentment. His prayer at the end of the passage is exactly Paul's heart in verses 15 to 18: remember me, my God, for good, according to all I have done for this people.

storyConnections.title: Abram Refuses the Spoils of Sodom
storyConnections.summary: After Abram rescued Lot and defeated the kings who had plundered Sodom, the king of Sodom offered him all the recovered goods. By the customs of war, Abram had every right to them. But Abram had just been blessed by Melchizedek, priest of God Most High, and he refused to take so much as a thread or a sandal strap, so that the king of Sodom could never say, “I have made Abram rich.” He allowed his allies to take their share, but he would not let anyone boast that his wealth came from a pagan king rather than from God. Paul's passion in verse 15 — that no one should make his boasting void — is the same instinct. Some rights are not worth taking, because of what others would say about the God you serve.

storyConnections.title: King Saul, Anointed and Rejected
storyConnections.summary: Saul began with every advantage. He was anointed by Samuel, the Spirit of God came on him, and he even prophesied among the prophets, so that people asked whether Saul was also among them. But he never learned to bring himself under God's command. He offered a sacrifice he was not authorised to offer because he was impatient. He spared the best of the Amalekite spoil when God had commanded total destruction, then claimed it was for sacrifice. And Samuel told him that to obey is better than sacrifice, and that because he had rejected the word of the LORD, the LORD had rejected him as king. Saul is the Old Testament picture of 1 Corinthians 9:27: a man who started in the Spirit, ministered to others, and was disqualified because he would not discipline his own will.
